universal_lens: The Delboeuf vertical bias manifests as a non-linear scaling operator acting on spatial manifolds. Ground-plane perspective induces an asymmetric Jacobian determinant, systematically inflating lower-hemisphere metric tensors. This geometric prior dictates how raw sensory coordinates are warped into perceived Euclidean distances.

reasoning_traces.think:
The derivation begins with the fundamental geometric constraint of human vision: objects are predominantly observed resting on a horizontal ground plane. Mathematically, this imposes a projective transformation where the lower half of the visual field consistently maps to greater physical distances than the upper half. To maintain size constancy, the cognitive system learns an inverse mapping—a scaling operator that artificially expands the metric tensor associated with the lower retinal hemisphere. When this deeply ingrained operator is applied to a strictly vertical stimulus, such as a line drawn on paper, the system erroneously assumes the lower segment is further away. Consequently, the perceived length of the lower half is inflated, causing the bisection point to be placed significantly higher than the true geometric center (the Delboeuf illusion). Wundt proposed an alternative mechanistic explanation rooted in physiological effort: the 'feeling of innervation.' He posited that the muscular force required to elevate the eyes creates a proprioceptive gradient, tricking the brain into perceiving the upper vertical distance as larger. However, Lipps successfully refuted this purely kinesthetic model by demonstrating that we do not perceive towering structures like steeples as gigantic simply because we look up at them. Therefore, the sovereign primitive must isolate the geometric prior—the ground-plane assumption—as the dominant operator, treating the innervation gradient as a secondary, context-dependent noise term that only applies to localized ocular saccades rather than global spatial perception.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This lineage traces back to Helmholtz’s unconscious inference, formalizing perception as a Bayesian inversion of optical physics. Delboeuf empirically quantified the resulting geometric asymmetry in 1879. Wundt subsequently attempted to ground this geometric distortion in measurable physiological mechanics (oculomotor innervation). Lipps provided the critical boundary condition, proving the physiological model insufficient for macroscopic spatial reasoning.
